workedExamples.stem:
Throughout, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular unit vectors, with $\mathbf{i}$ along the positive x-axis.

Three forces act on a body: $(9\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-5\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N and $(8\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N.

(i) Find the resultant of the three forces.
(ii) Calculate its magnitude.
(iii) Calculate the angle it makes with the positive x-axis. Round to 2 decimal places.

figure.alt: A table of three forces written in i and j with their across and up parts listed: 9 and minus 4, minus 5 and 7, and 8 and 2. The bottom row totals the two columns to give a resultant of 12 across and 5 up.

steps.decision: Total one column at a time. Adding $-5$ takes five away, which is where the sign slips happen.

steps.working: So the resultant is $12\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}$ N, since the $\mathbf{j}$ parts give $-4 + 7 + 2 = 5$.
steps.decision: Nothing crosses between the columns, so the second total is worked out on its own and then written beside the first.

options: Because across and up are independent directions
Because the two columns must be added together at the end
Because the resultant is always a single number
whyMenu.explain: A step to the right never moves you up, so the two totals stay apart. The single number comes later, as the magnitude.

steps.decision: The two totals are perpendicular, so the magnitude is the longest side of their right-angled triangle.

steps.working: Measured from the positive x-axis, the angle $= \tan^{-1}\dfrac{5}{12} = 22.62°$.
steps.decision: The up total is opposite the angle, so it goes on top. Measuring from the x-axis is what the question asked for.

steps.decision: Take right as positive, so the 10 N force is subtracted. The 24 N force is at an angle, so only its cosine part lies along this direction.
The two horizontal forces contribute nothing upwards, so only the angled force appears in this total.
The unrounded totals go into the calculator, and only the final answer is rounded.

options: Because rounding twice moves the answer away from the value the scheme wants
Because the totals are not needed once the magnitude is found
Because the magnitude must be a whole number
whyMenu.explain: Each rounding shifts a value slightly. Rounding the totals and then squaring them can move the final figure in the second decimal place.

twin.stem:
A body has a total component of $24$ N to the right and $7$ N upwards. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant.

Answer ________ N

items.stem: From an earlier topic: work out $-4 + 7 + 2$.

options.feedback: Adding 7 to $-4$ gives 3, and 2 more gives 5.
That treats the $-4$ as $+4$.
That subtracts both of the other numbers.
That leaves the 2 out.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a right-angled triangle has shorter sides of $8$ and $6$. How long is the longest side?

options.feedback: That adds the two sides, which would only be right if they pointed the same way.
That is the sum of the squares, before the square root.
That doubles each side instead of squaring it: $2 \times 8 + 2 \times 6 = 28$.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: in a right-angled triangle the side opposite an angle is $5$ and the side beside it is $12$. Which expression gives the angle?

options.feedback: Tangent is opposite over adjacent, so the 5 goes on top.
That is the other angle in the same triangle.
Sine needs the longest side underneath, not the adjacent one.
That would take the tangent of a number rather than finding the angle.

items.stem: Three forces of $30$ N, $24$ N and $10$ N act at a point in different directions. Which statement about their resultant is correct?

options.text: its magnitude is less than $64$ N
options.feedback: Forces only add to their total when they point the same way.
That totals the sizes and ignores the directions altogether.

options.text: it has a magnitude but no direction
options.feedback: A resultant is a force, so it has both, and an answer needs both.

options.text: it acts along the largest of the three forces
options.feedback: Every force affects the direction of the resultant, not just the largest.

items.stem: What is the resultant of $(7\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-4\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ N?

options.feedback: $7 - 4 = 3$ across and $-3 + 8 = 5$ up.
That subtracts the second force instead of adding it.
The $-3$ has lost its sign: adding 8 to $-3$ gives 5, not 11.
The $-4$ has lost its sign: adding it takes four away.

items.skill: Totalling components that face each other
items.stem: One force has a component of $18$ N to the right and another has a component of $25$ N to the left. What is the total component to the right?

options.feedback: $18 - 25 = -7$ N, so the total of 7 N actually points to the left.
Adding treats the second component as helping the first.
The size is right but the sign is not: taking right as positive, the total is negative.
Components are added and subtracted, never multiplied.

items.stem: The forces on a body total $9$ N to the right and $12$ N upwards. What is the magnitude of the resultant?

options.feedback: That adds the two totals. They act at right angles, so the resultant is shorter than their sum.
That is the sum of the squares. The square root is the last step.
That is the larger total on its own, with the other one left out.

items.stem: The forces on a body total $9$ N to the right and $12$ N upwards. Which expression gives the angle the resultant makes with the horizontal?

options.feedback: The up total is opposite the angle from the horizontal, so it goes on top.
That is the angle with the vertical. The reports name this reciprocal as the commonest error in the direction part.
Sine needs the resultant underneath, and a sine can never be greater than one.
Cosine also needs the resultant underneath, and the fraction is greater than one.

parts.stem:
A buoy is pulled by a rope with a force of $22$ N at $35°$ above the horizontal, to the right, and by a second rope with a force of $14$ N horizontally to the left.

Calculate the total component of the two forces to the right. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Resolve the slanted pull first.
The second rope pulls the other way.

commonErrors.feedback: The resolved component is right, so the method mark (M) stands, but the second rope pulls to the left and is subtracted.
That uses the whole $22$ N. Only $22\cos 35°$ of it lies along the horizontal.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total component of the two forces upwards. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: The horizontal rope contributes nothing upwards.
parts.workedSolution: Only the first rope has an upward part: $22\sin 35° = 12.62$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $22\cos 35°$, the part along the horizontal. Upwards is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine.

parts.stem:

parts.stem:
Three forces act at a point $O$, as shown. A force of $25$ N acts horizontally to the right, a force of $19$ N acts at $65°$ above the horizontal and to the right, and a force of $12$ N acts horizontally to the left.

Calculate the total component of the three forces to the right. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Resolve the angled force first.
Take the direction to the right as positive.

commonErrors.feedback: The resolved component is right, which earns the method mark (M), but the $12$ N force pulls the other way and is subtracted.
That puts the whole $19$ N into the horizontal total. Only $19\cos 65°$ of it acts that way.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total component of the three forces upwards. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Two of the three forces are horizontal.
parts.workedSolution: Only the $19$ N force has an upward part: $19\sin 65° = 17.22$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $19\cos 65°$, the part along the horizontal. Upwards is opposite the angle and takes the sine.
That totals all three forces as though direction did not matter. Only the part of each force that points upwards belongs in this total.

parts.stem:
Calculate the magnitude of the resultant of the three forces. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: the two totals squared, added and rooted

hints: Keep the unrounded totals in the calculator.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds the two totals. They act at right angles, so they combine by Pythagoras.
That is the sum of the squares, so the method mark (M) stands. The square root finishes it.

parts.stem:
Calculate the angle the resultant makes with the horizontal. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: the inverse tangent of the upward total over the rightward total

hints: The upward total is opposite the angle from the horizontal.

commonErrors.feedback: That fraction is the wrong way up and gives the angle with the vertical. The question names the horizontal.
That is the magnitude again. A direction is an angle, worked out from the two totals rather than from their combined size.

findTheMistake.stem: Rhys is finding the resultant of the forces $(6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N. His working:
studentWorking: the resultant is the sum of the forces
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 subtracts the second force's $\mathbf{j}$ part where line 1 says the forces are added. The $\mathbf{i}$ line is right: $-5$ is already negative, so adding it takes five away. The $\mathbf{j}$ line should add 9 to $-2$ and give 7.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the resultant as the sum and keeping the two columns apart is the method, and it earns the method mark (M). One operation applies to the whole vector: if the i line adds, the j line adds too. Writing the two forces one above the other before you start makes a stray sign hard to miss.

prompts.prompt: What is the resultant of a set of forces?
prompts.answer: The single force that would have exactly the same effect on the body as the whole set.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the resultant of forces given in i and j form?
prompts.answer: Total the i parts and total the j parts, keeping the two columns apart and the signs with their numbers.

prompts.prompt: What is the first step when the forces are given at angles rather than in components?
prompts.answer: Resolve every force into two perpendicular directions, usually the horizontal and the vertical.

prompts.prompt: The forces on a body total X to the right and Y upwards. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
prompts.answer: The square root of X squared plus Y squared, which is on the Unit 2 formula sheet.

prompts.prompt: The forces on a body total X to the right and Y upwards. What angle does the resultant make with the horizontal?
prompts.answer: The inverse tangent of Y over X, with the upward total on top.

prompts.prompt: Why is the resultant of three forces of 30 N, 24 N and 10 N never 64 N unless they are parallel?
prompts.answer: Because forces only add to their total when they point the same way; otherwise part of each works against the others.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for the direction of a resultant. What is the commonest way marks are lost?
prompts.answer: Turning the fraction over, which gives the angle with the vertical instead of the angle with the horizontal.
